notes.meaning: David had six sons during the years he ruled in the city of Hebron, each by a different wife. His second son, Daniel, is called Chileab in the book of Samuel. Several of these sons, especially Absalom and Adonijah, later brought great heartbreak and rebellion to David's household.

David ruled in Hebron for seven and a half years before moving his capital to Jerusalem, where he reigned for thirty-three years. Hebron was the center of his rule over Judah alone. Moving to Jerusalem marked the uniting of all twelve tribes under God's chosen king.

Four sons were born to David in Jerusalem by Bathsheba, who is called Bath-shua here. Solomon is listed last even though he received the throne, because the rest of the royal family tree continues through him. Nathan is also notable because the New Testament later traces Jesus' family line through him as well.

David had nine other sons born in Jerusalem through his other wives. Two names appear twice in the list, likely because older sons died in childhood and their names were given to later sons to honor their memory. David gave these sons names that praised God, such as Eliphelet, which means 'God is deliverance.'

These sons were born to David's primary wives, though he also had other sons by concubines, who were secondary wives. Tamar is the only daughter named in the record because of her tragic and famous place in the story of David's family.

Solomon's line of kings in Judah passed down in direct succession from father to son for many generations. The list includes both godly leaders like Asa and Jehoshaphat and wicked rulers like Joram and Ahaziah. The usurper Athaliah took the throne by force for six years, but she is left out here because she was not of David's line.

The royal succession continued through Ahaz to good king Hezekiah, then through Manasseh and Amon down to the reformer king Josiah. Even during times when wicked kings led the nation astray, God remained faithful to His promise to preserve David's royal line.

Four sons of Josiah are listed, three of whom became kings during Judah's final, chaotic years before the fall of Jerusalem. Foreign empires began setting up and deposing kings, breaking the normal pattern of the oldest son succeeding his father. Jeconiah was carried away captive to Babylon, and his uncle Zedekiah became the last reigning king of Judah.

Jeconiah is called 'the captive' because he was taken as a prisoner to Babylon. The prophet Jeremiah had warned that no son of Jeconiah would prosper on the throne, but God still preserved his family and allowed him to have children in exile. Seven of his sons or descendants born during the captivity are recorded here.

Zerubbabel was the leader who helped bring the Jewish exiles back to Jerusalem to rebuild the temple. He is named here as the son of Pedaiah, though other passages call him the son of Shealtiel, likely because Shealtiel adopted him or died childless. Zerubbabel gave his children names full of hope, such as Jushab-hesed, which means 'mercy will be restored.'

These names trace several generations of David's family who lived after the return from Babylon. Hattush is mentioned in the book of Ezra as one of the leaders of David's house who returned from exile. Even though David's family no longer held a crown or royal palace, God's people kept careful records of the line.

The chapter closes by tracing David's descendants down through Neariah and Elioenai to seven final sons. These names bring the family history down to the end of Old Testament times, several centuries before Christ. God quietly kept the line of David alive in ordinary life until the true King, Jesus, arrived.
